html:
The episodic system is built from a set of semi-segregated cortical-MTL modules that specialize for complementary ingredients of an event-the "who/what," the "where/when/context," and the control signals that determine when to construct, retrieve, or reshape an episode. A useful organizing principle is the anterior-temporal versus posterior-medial (AT-PM) framework: an AT network centered on perirhinal cortex (PrC), anterior temporal lobe, and lateral orbitofrontal cortex emphasizes item-, person-, and concept-centric features, whereas a PM network centered on parahippocampal cortex (PHC), retrosplenial/precuneus, and posterior cingulate emphasizes scene and extended contextual structure 1. A network study compares proposed and data-driven divisions (Figure) 23.

These streams converge on the entorhinal cortex (EC) and hippocampus but remain partly segregated up to specific hippocampal subfield zones, enabling the system to bind item and context without collapsing their codes. In humans, anterior-lateral EC (alEC; homologous to rodent LEC) preferentially carries nonspatial information, providing information about objects, features, and the temporal context of events, while posterior-medial EC (pmEC; homologous to MEC) carries spatial/path-integration information, providing a multimodal spatial map of one’s environment; their projections target largely distinct sectors of CA1 along the proximodistal axis (LEC->distal CA1/subiculum, MEC->proximal CA1), preserving the division of labor as information enters the hippocampus 2, 3.

Perirhinal and parahippocampal cortices form the principal cortical interfaces to EC. PrC supports highly specific, object-centric and concept-rich representations and is well positioned to "unitize" features of an entity, often carrying learned value/affect through its amygdala connectivity. PHC (and the parahippocampal place area) emphasizes scenes, landmarks, and broader situational context, providing a scaffold for event location and environmental structure. Together these streams deliver entities and roles into EC, where they can be indexed by the hippocampus during encoding and reinstated during recall 4, 5, 6. An experiment tests retrieval of event content and context (Figure) 24. The experiment identifies cortical networks associated with memory (Figure).

A prominent gradient runs along the longitudinal (posterior-anterior) axis of the hippocampus and adjacent MTL, mirroring an abstraction/scale gradient in the computations that support episodes. Posterior hippocampus (dorsal in rodents) is biased toward fine-grained spatial detail, precise sequences, and smaller spatiotemporal scales; anterior hippocampus (ventral in rodents) emphasizes broader, gist-like, schematic, and affect-laden context, and is preferentially engaged when tasks are open-ended, prospective, or demand flexible recombination rather than cue-driven recall constrained by sensory specifics. Thus, the hippocampus is not monolithic: it embodies a multiscale memory system wherein the posterior end encodes the specific "episodes" with rich detail and the anterior end encodes more abstracted "situations" or schemas spanning episodes - a design that permits both episodic specificity and cross-episode generalization within a single circuit. This gradient maps onto entorhinal subdivisions and large-scale network coupling, with posterior sectors aligning more strongly to PM scene networks and anterior sectors to AT/valuation networks 7, 8, 9. The study compares connectivity along the hippocampal axis (Figure).

Beyond MTL, the "core recollection network" supporting vivid episodic remembering overlaps extensively with the default mode network (DMN), with special emphasis on its midline core: anterior medial prefrontal cortex (amPFC) and posterior cingulate/precuneus (PCC). These hubs sit high in the cortical semantic hierarchy and maintain event context during both on-line perception and recall, projecting schematic event models onto new input to generate predictions. The amPFC (including ventromedial PFC) is strongly engaged when memories have personal relevance or schematic structure - it may inject self-referential and schema-based information into the reconstruction of a scene, encoding one’s goals, identity, and prior knowledge into the remembered event. This region is also implicated in scene construction and imagination, as neuroimaging shows amPFC activity when people envision novel experiences or place themselves in hypothetical scenarios, in concert with hippocampal activation. Meanwhile, the posterior cingulate cortex (encompassing PCC proper and retrosplenial areas) serves as a hub linking hippocampal outputs to widespread cortical regions. The PCC is believed to support the spatiotemporal context and vivid re-experiencing of memory scenes; for example, damage to retrosplenial cortex impairs the ability to mentally navigate familiar places or recall rich contextual details. During recollection, PCC shows increased connectivity with the hippocampus and parietal cortex 10, and it may help integrate egocentric (self-centered) perspective with the allocentric (world-centered) representations coming from the hippocampus, grounding recalled events in a coherent viewpoint or "scene" from the autobiographical self.

The angular gyrus (a lateral parietal region) has emerged as a critical locus for integrating the content elements of a memory into a single conscious experience. Cognitive models propose that AG functions as an "episodic buffer" or convergence zone, where the various components of an event - sights, sounds, people, places, emotions - are bound together and brought to awareness as a unified memory 11, 12. Consistent with this, high-resolution fMRI multivariate analyses have shown that during episodic retrieval (especially after memories have been consolidated), different feature-specific representations reconverge in the angular gyrus 10. The AG is also strongly associated with the subjective sense of recollection - patients often report less vivid or "complete" recall when the lateral parietal cortex is disrupted, despite being able to recognize or know that something happened. Causal evidence for AG’s role in memory vividness comes from brain stimulation studies: applying inhibitory TMS to left angular gyrus prior to retrieval selectively reduces the vividness of recollected memories without affecting objective accuracy or metacognitive confidence 13. This indicates that while the hippocampus provides the core content (and can support basic recognition even if AG is offline), the angular gyrus contributes critical multimodal integration and rich re-experiential detail - effectively painting the full scene and embedding it in our awareness. Along with parietal hub regions, primary and premotor cortices can be recruited when episodes involve planned or simulated actions, reflecting the embodied, interactive nature of event construction 14. A white-matter atlas visualizes the fornix (Figure) 25. A 2026 anatomy review maps limbic and language-related tracts (Figure) 26.

Remembering is not always a passive replay; often it is a goal-directed act of retrieval guided by the prefrontal cortex (PFC). Both medial and lateral prefrontal regions are recruited to initiate memory search, apply learned schemas, and monitor the products of retrieval. The medial PFC, especially the ventromedial PFC (vmPFC), interacts closely with the hippocampus during encoding and recall of schema-related memories. This region encodes high-level contextual or schematic representations - abstract frameworks that organize knowledge - and can use these to bias hippocampal retrieval toward schema-consistent information 10. Studies have shown that vmPFC activity can precede and drive hippocampal activity when a person starts to recall an autobiographical memory: in MEG recordings, vmPFC activation was seen to lead hippocampal reinstatement at the onset of memory retrieval, suggesting the PFC provides an early cue or "trigger" that kicks off hippocampal pattern completion 15. The vmPFC likely carries a summary of one’s current goals and prior knowledge, which helps instigate and coordinate hippocampal-dependent recall processes. During encoding, strong hippocampal-vmPFC coupling has been associated with the schema effect - better learning of new information that fits an existing schema - supporting theories that the PFC actively assimilates new episodes into organized knowledge networks 16. During retrieval, the vmPFC also plays a role in reality monitoring and selection: patients with vmPFC damage can retrieve many details from memory but are prone to confabulation, weaving together pieces that don’t belong or endorsing false memories, presumably because the control processes that evaluate and constrain retrieved information are compromised 17. This highlights that medial PFC normally helps ensure that the recalled scenario is coherent and relevant to the query, suppressing extraneous associations and filling gaps with plausible elements (often based on schemas or semantic memory) rather than false blends.

Complementing the medial PFC, the lateral prefrontal cortex (especially dorsolateral PFC) provides executive control over search and verification operations during episodic recall. The lateral PFC is engaged when we must intentionally search our memory (e.g. "recall everything that happened at last week’s meeting"), maintaining task cues and systematically probing memory stores. It helps formulate effective retrieval strategies (such as initiating recall by time or place cues), and it dynamically focuses hippocampal retrieval by inhibiting irrelevant memory traces. The dorsolateral PFC (DLPFC), in particular, is associated with post-retrieval monitoring - checking whether the content retrieved is what was sought and is veridical. If the hippocampus produces partial or ambiguous results, the DLPFC can cue another attempt or cross-check details against expectations (analogous to an internal query refinement loop). Together, these prefrontal mechanisms impose a hierarchical control on episodic recall: high-level goals and semantic constraints (often represented in anterior/medial PFC) guide the general direction of retrieval, while mid-ventrolateral PFC may retrieve specific cues or semantic seeds, and dorsolateral PFC evaluates and edits the output. Recent computational models formalize this idea, positing that the PFC generates "queries" to the hippocampus in a top-down manner - effectively encoding a cue or key that will trigger hippocampal pattern completion of a relevant memory - and then gates the retrieved memory for use in decision-making 18. The PFC also works in concert with the hippocampus for episodic simulation - assembling elements from past events to imagine novel futures (more on this later) - by enforcing constraints so that imagined scenarios remain realistic and in line with one’s goals. In summary, the medial and lateral PFC together form an executive layer that queries, guides, and validates the hippocampal memory retrieval, enabling episodic memory to function not just as a recording device but as a flexible, queryable database for decision-making and planning.

The effectiveness of memory encoding and retrieval is profoundly influenced by reward, emotion, and other salience signals, implemented via interactions between the hippocampus and subcortical neuromodulatory centers. One important pathway is the hippocampus-midbrain dopaminergic loop, which links novelty and reward evaluation to memory formation. When the hippocampus detects something novel or unexpected in the environment, it can trigger a burst of dopamine from the ventral tegmental area (VTA); this dopamine release, in turn, enhances synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus, prioritizing the encoding of that event 19. Individual differences in the integrity of this loop (for example, structural connectivity between midbrain and hippocampus) correlate with how well people remember rewarded information. Complementing dopamine’s role, emotional arousal engages the amygdala - another key subcortical player - which modulates episodic memory via stress and arousal hormones. The amygdala-hippocampus interaction is known to boost memory for emotionally charged events: during emotional experiences, the amygdala can influence hippocampal circuits both directly and through neurochemical cascades (such as norepinephrine release from the locus coeruleus) 20, with recent intracranial work showing amygdala-theta to hippocampal-gamma coupling that predicts subsequent memory for aversive scenes 21. Finally, the hippocampal system interfaces with the basal ganglia to translate memory into action, particularly via the nucleus accumbens (NAc) in the ventral striatum. The hippocampus->NAc pathway (largely from ventral subiculum) provides the striatum with contextual and spatial information about experiences, effectively informing the reward system of "where" and "what" has happened 22. The NAc, in turn, is a motivation hub that helps select behaviors based on expected rewards. Animal studies show that this pathway is necessary for linking memories to motivated behavior: if hippocampal outputs to NAcc are silenced, animals cannot learn or express place-reward associations (e.g. remembering a location where food was found).
